candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — collaborative healthcare outbreak investigation
candidate.educational_objective: Participate in outbreak response as a systematic, collaborative process of case verification and finding, descriptive and analytic epidemiology, hypothesis testing, and timely implementation of evidence-informed control measures.

options.A: Verify the diagnoses and outbreak, alert key partners, define and find cases, analyze data by person/place/time, develop and test hypotheses, and implement control measures as evidence becomes available.
options.B: Select the most likely source immediately and design all control actions around that assumption without systematic case finding or data analysis.
options.C: Wait until the cluster becomes large before beginning an investigation because smaller clusters do not warrant epidemiologic assessment.
options.D: Keep the investigation within the public-health team and avoid collaboration with facility clinicians, laboratory personnel, and infection-prevention staff.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes outbreak and healthcare-associated infection investigations as systematic, multistep processes that include verifying the diagnosis and outbreak, communicating with key partners, establishing case definitions, identifying and counting cases, organizing data by person, place, and time, formulating and testing hypotheses, implementing control measures, and communicating findings. Steps may occur concurrently, and preliminary control measures may be appropriate before the entire investigation is complete. B anchors prematurely without evidence. C is incorrect because even a single unusual healthcare-associated case can trigger a full investigation depending on the disease and setting. D conflicts with CDC's emphasis on collaboration among public-health officials, facility staff, clinicians, laboratories, and other stakeholders.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Healthcare outbreak investigations use a systematic, collaborative sequence of diagnosis/outbreak verification, case definition and finding, descriptive analysis, hypothesis development/testing, control measures, and communication; steps may overlap and smaller signals can still warrant investigation.
